clues: It commits a six-carbon sugar to breakdown inside the cytosol.
Citrate and high ATP slow it down, while AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate speed it up.
It is the main rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis that converts fructose 6-phosphate into fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
It is a regulatory signal molecule rather than a direct intermediate of energy production.
Insulin raises its hepatic levels after a meal, while glucagon causes it to be broken down.
It is the most potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 and inhibitor of fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase.
This hepatic enzyme only works at full speed right after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
Unlike its counterpart in other tissues, it is not inhibited by its own phosphorylated product.
It is the high-Km, high-Vmax hexokinase isozyme found in liver parenchymal cells and pancreatic beta cells.
It acts as the irreversible one-way bridge between cytosolic sugar breakdown and mitochondrial oxidation.
It requires five cofactors, including thiamine pyrophosphate and lipoic acid.
This mitochondrial multienzyme complex converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, NADH, and carbon dioxide.
It is the only enzyme of its cycle that is not dissolved freely in the mitochondrial matrix.
Malonate acts as its classic structural competitive inhibitor.
This inner membrane enzyme oxidizes succinate to fumarate and also serves as Complex II of the electron transport chain.
It performs a crucial anaplerotic reaction inside mitochondria when energy is low.
It requires biotin to fix carbon dioxide and is completely inactive without acetyl-CoA.
This enzyme converts pyruvate into oxaloacetate as the first bypass step of gluconeogenesis.
It prevents muscle fatigue by clearing an acidic byproduct through the bloodstream.
It shifts the metabolic burden of anaerobic exercise onto the liver at a net cost of four ATP.
This metabolic loop transports lactate from exercising muscle to the liver to be converted back into glucose.
It breaks down a branched storage polymer without spending any ATP.
It uses inorganic phosphate and requires pyridoxal phosphate as a covalently bound cofactor.
This rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds to release glucose 1-phosphate.
It sits right at the very center of every cellular carbohydrate storage granule.
It acts as both an enzyme and its own substrate by attaching sugars to a tyrosine residue.
This self-glucosylating protein forms the short oligosaccharide primer needed to start glycogen synthesis.
Affected infants present with doll-like faces, enlarged livers, and severe fasting low blood sugar.
Trapped phosphorylated sugar leads to lactic acidosis, high triglycerides, and gouty uric acid levels.
This Type I glycogen storage disease is caused by a deficiency of glucose 6-phosphatase.

terms.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
clues: Its deficiency is the most common human enzymopathy and offers protection against severe malaria.
Exposure to fava beans or primaquine triggers Heinz bodies and bite cells when it is lacking.
This rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH to keep glutathione reduced.

terms.sub: Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Monosaccharide Metabolism
clues: Measuring its activity in red blood cells is a clinical laboratory test for thiamine deficiency.
It operates in the reversible non-oxidative branch of the hexose monophosphate shunt.
This thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent enzyme transfers two-carbon units between ketose and aldose sugars.

terms.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
clues: Unlike cytochromes, this electron carrier is a hydrophobic lipid-soluble quinone rather than a protein.
It roams freely inside the inner mitochondrial membrane collecting reducing equivalents.
Also known as ubiquinone, it accepts electrons from both Complex I and Complex II and passes them to Complex III.

terms.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
clues: It allows newborns and hibernating animals to stay warm without shivering.
Norepinephrine triggers fatty acid release to open this inner mitochondrial membrane channel.
Also called uncoupling protein 1 in brown adipose tissue, it dissipates the proton gradient to generate heat.

terms.sub: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
clues: This macrolide antibiotic halts cellular energy production by jamming a rotary proton channel.
Adding an uncoupler like dinitrophenol restores oxygen consumption after it blocks respiration.
It inhibits oxidative phosphorylation by directly binding the Fo subunit of ATP synthase.
Citrate polymerizes and activates it, whereas AMPK phosphorylates and shuts it down.
It uses biotin and ATP to add a carboxyl group in the cytosol.
This rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis converts acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA.
It serves as the two-carbon building block donor during lipogenesis.
Its levels rise after a meal to prevent a futile cycle of simultaneous lipid synthesis and breakdown.
This product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase allosterically inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I.
Despite its traditional classification, it is chemically a carboxylic acid that lacks a ketone group.
It rises dramatically in diabetic ketoacidosis but goes undetected by standard urine nitroprusside strips.
It is the most abundant circulating ketone body produced in liver mitochondria and oxidized by the starving brain.
Statins competitively block this endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme to lower blood lipids.
High cellular sterols suppress its gene transcription via the SCAP-SREBP-2 sensor.
It is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol biosynthesis that reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonate.
Chylomicrons and VLDL must borrow this surface protein from HDL after entering the bloodstream.
Its genetic deficiency causes massive hypertriglyceridemia and eruptive xanthomas.
This apolipoprotein acts as an essential cofactor to activate capillary lipoprotein lipase.
It mediates neutral lipid swapping between circulating lipoproteins in plasma.
Genetic deficiency of this protein leads to markedly elevated HDL cholesterol levels.
This plasma transfer protein moves cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL and LDL in exchange for triglycerides.
It is abundant in snake venoms and pancreatic secretions.
Corticosteroids induce annexin A1 to block this enzyme and shut down inflammation.
This enzyme hydrolyzes the sn-2 ester bond of membrane phospholipids to release arachidonic acid.

terms.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
clues: It works inside hepatocyte mitochondria rather than the cytosol.
It is completely inactive unless N-acetylglutamate binds to it.
This rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle combines free ammonia, bicarbonate, and two ATP molecules.

terms.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
clues: Deficiency of this enzyme is the most common urea cycle disorder and is inherited in an X-linked manner.
Affected neonates develop hyperammonemia alongside elevated urinary orotic acid.
This mitochondrial enzyme condenses carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline.

terms.sub: Amino Acid Catabolism and Urea Cycle
clues: Patients develop blue-black ear cartilage pigmentation and painful arthritis in adulthood.
Freshly passed urine looks normal but turns dark black after standing exposed to air.
This autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine catabolism is caused by homogentisate oxidase deficiency.
Barbiturates induce its hepatic isoform, which can precipitate acute porphyria attacks.
Heme feedback-inhibits its synthesis and mitochondrial import.
This pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA in the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis.
Stress, illness, or exam-week fasting brings out mild yellowing of the eyes in otherwise healthy young adults.
Liver enzymes and red cell counts remain completely normal.
This benign condition causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to reduced UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 activity.
Affected boys exhibit severe gout, spasticity, and compulsive self-mutilating biting.
Orange uric acid crystals often appear in the infant's diaper.
This X-linked disorder is caused by deficiency of the purine salvage enzyme HGPRT.
